analysis.one_liner: Ends the legal exception letting employers pay disabled workers less than minimum wage, with grants to help employers transition.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on February 28, 2023 and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, employers can get a "special certificate" (Section 14(c)) allowing them to pay workers with disabilities below the federal minimum wage — sometimes just a few dollars an hour. This bill would have ended that: no new certificates, a four-year wage phase-in for existing ones, and federal grants to help states and employers convert to jobs where disabled workers earn at least the regular minimum wage alongside non-disabled co-workers. It was never acted on by the committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with disabilities who are currently paid below minimum wage under Section 14(c) certificates would gain the right to at least the federal minimum wage, phased in over four years, plus help finding mainstream jobs. The bill also earmarks transition grants to the employers and states, so the employers bearing the change get public money to convert their business models rather than having to close overnight.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Disabled workers now paid below minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: Phases out special certificates over four years: new ones are banned immediately and existing ones lose legal effect four years after enactment, ending legal payment of subminimum wages to disabled workers.
Before the sunset, wages of certificate holders must rise step by step — 60% of the federal minimum in year one, then 70%, 80%, 90%, and full minimum wage by year four.

Creates federal grants so employers and states can convert their business models to competitive integrated employment with support services, rather than simply losing their legal ability to pay below minimum wage.
Funds technical assistance for employers and an independent evaluation of what happens to disabled workers' wages and employment after the transition.

analysis.who_pays: Employers currently holding 14(c) certificates — mostly nonprofit sheltered workshops and some government contractors — would lose the ability to pay disabled workers subminimum wages, though federal transition grants would subsidize the changeover; taxpayers would fund the $50 million annual grant program.

drawbacks.text: Some sheltered-workshop operators and some families argue that workers with the most significant disabilities cannot find or hold competitive jobs, and that the subminimum wage was what kept those programs open at all.

The transition grants were authorized at $50 million a year but not guaranteed — Congress still had to appropriate the money each year, and no funding stream was attached to the employers' loss of the 14(c) wage exception itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is strong on fairness: a subminimum wage for disabled workers is hard to defend once stated plainly, and the four-year ramp plus transformation grants showed real concern for the sheltered workshops' survival rather than an abrupt shutdown. The honest objection is that transitions can fail for individual workers — the highest-support workers might lose hours, pay, or their community — and the grants were authorized but not guaranteed appropriations. On balance the bill offered a gradual, funded path to a legal wage floor for a group now legally paid less than everyone else, and the cost of the transition falls mostly on employers who currently profit from the exception. It died without a committee vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and never moved — no hearing, no vote, in either chamber — and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 28, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
That was the only action ever taken; no hearing, markup, or floor vote occurred in the 118th Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill advancing, so the subminimum-wage exception for disabled workers remained in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sheltered workshops and other employers holding 14(c) certificates are better off: they keep the legal right to pay disabled workers less than minimum wage, with no transition required.

for.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
for.role: Sponsor, House Education and Workforce Committee ranking member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase out the 14(c) subminimum wage program and fund the transition.

for.name: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers
for.role: Original cosponsor, chair of the House Republican Conference
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its Republican co-lead.

for.name: 31 of 216 House Democrats and 3 of 224 House Republicans

against.name: Sheltered workshop operators and some provider organizations
against.what_they_did: Providers that pay disabled workers under special certificates have generally opposed phasing out the 14(c) program, arguing some workers cannot work in competitive settings.

against.name: Some parents and family members of workers in sheltered workshops
against.what_they_did: Some families publicly opposed ending subminimum-wage certificates, fearing their family members would lose structured employment settings.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had sponsors from both parties — a Democratic sponsor and a senior Republican cosponsor — but support was thin: 34 cosponsors out of 435 House members, and the Republican-led committee never took it up.

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and disability day-services providers holding 14(c) certificates
industries.note: The bill ends the legal ability to pay disabled workers below minimum wage and, for certificate holders that take grants, requires converting to integrated employment models. Their interest in keeping 14(c) ran against the workers they employed.
These employers operate heavily on 14(c) certificates and pay disabled workers under minimum wage on federal contracts; the phaseout raises their labor costs over four years.

industries.industry: Disability employment-services providers that already offer competitive integrated employment
industries.note: Providers already doing integrated employment would receive grants and ongoing state funding to absorb workers transferring out of sheltered workshops, locking in their role as the support system.
